title: (Scenario) A critical service has grown to 300,000 lines of code — would you split it into microservices, and what would you evaluate BEFORE deciding (which modules change together, where ownership is unclear, whether failures in one capability affect unrelated capabilities, and whether improving internal boundaries solves the pain without introducing network communication, distributed tracing, service discovery, and cross-service data consistency)?
shortTitle: A critical service has grown to 300,000 lines — would you split it into microservices, and what would you evaluate first?

s1_definition.profdef: Size alone is not a reason to split a service; the decision should follow evidence about coupling, ownership, and blast radius, not line count. Before splitting you evaluate which modules change together (change coupling), where ownership is ambiguous, and whether a failure in one capability takes down unrelated capabilities. Crucially you ask whether the real pain can be solved by strengthening internal module boundaries inside the single deployable, because splitting converts in-process method calls into network calls and imports a permanent tax of distributed tracing, service discovery, retries, and cross-service data consistency. You split only where there is a concrete boundary that the current monolith cannot provide — independent deployment, independent scaling, fault isolation, or separate ownership — and you split along that seam, not arbitrarily.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India runs one very large branch that handles loans, transfers, and fraud checks all under one roof. It has grown huge and feels unwieldy. The question is not "it is big, so build three branches." The question is: which activities actually get in each other's way, who is responsible for what, and does a problem in the loans desk ever stop the transfers desk from working? Often the fix is to reorganise the one big branch into clearly separated departments with their own doors and managers. You only open a genuinely separate branch when a department truly needs its own building — its own hours, its own staff, its own ability to stay open when another burns down.
s1_definition.oneliner: Line count is not a reason to split; split only where you have evidence of independent change, ownership, scaling, or failure needs that a stronger internal boundary cannot satisfy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Size alone is not a reason to split a service; the decision should follow evidence about coupling, ownership, and blast radius, not line count. Before splitting you evaluate which modules change together (change coupling), where ownership is ambiguous, and whether a failure in one capability takes down unrelated capabilities. Crucially you ask whether the real pain can be solved by strengthening internal module boundaries inside the single deployable, because splitting converts in-process method calls into network calls and imports a permanent tax of distributed tracing, service discovery, retries, and cross-service data consistency. You split only where there is a concrete boundary that the current monolith cannot provide — independent deployment, independent scaling, fault isolation, or separate ownership — and you split along that seam, not arbitrarily.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India runs one very large branch that handles loans, transfers, and fraud checks all under one roof. It has grown huge and feels unwieldy. The question is not "it is big, so build three branches." The question is: which activities actually get in each other's way, who is responsible for what, and does a problem in the loans desk ever stop the transfers desk from working? Often the fix is to reorganise the one big branch into clearly separated departments with their own doors and managers. You only open a genuinely separate branch when a department truly needs its own building — its own hours, its own staff, its own ability to stay open when another burns down.

**One line to remember:** Line count is not a reason to split; split only where you have evidence of independent change, ownership, scaling, or failure needs that a stronger internal boundary cannot satisfy.

sections.s2_technical:
The first thing I evaluate is change coupling: which modules change together in the same commits and pull requests. If loan-origination and loan-servicing almost always change together, splitting them into two services does not reduce complexity — it spreads a single logical change across two deployables, two pipelines, and a network boundary, making every change slower and riskier. The modules that are good split candidates are the ones that change independently of the rest, because only those gain independent deployment. You can measure this from version-control history by looking at which files co-change.

The second thing is ownership. A split pays off when it aligns a service with a team that owns it end to end, so that team can deploy and operate it without coordinating with others. If ownership is unclear — if no single team would own the extracted service — the split creates an orphan that everyone depends on and nobody maintains, which is worse than a module inside a monolith. Conway's Law cuts both ways here: services should mirror team boundaries, so I evaluate whether the proposed services match how teams are actually organised.

The third thing is blast radius: does a failure or a resource spike in one capability affect unrelated capabilities today? If a runaway report generation can exhaust the heap and take down transfers, that is real fault coupling that a split could fix by isolating the report capability into its own process with its own resources. But if capabilities are already well isolated by threading and resource limits inside the monolith, a split buys little fault isolation at high cost.

The fourth thing is independent scaling. If one capability needs to scale very differently from the rest — say fraud scoring is CPU-heavy and bursty while account lookups are steady — splitting lets you scale them independently. If everything scales together, a split gives no scaling benefit.

Against all of these I weigh the permanent tax that microservices import. In-process method calls become network calls that can be slow, fail, or time out, so you need retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers everywhere a call used to be a simple method invocation. You need service discovery so services can find each other, distributed tracing so you can follow one request across process boundaries, and you lose the single database transaction — a change that spanned two modules atomically now spans two services and needs sagas, outbox patterns, and eventual consistency. This is not a one-time cost; it is a tax on every future change and every incident.

The senior nuance is that most "we need microservices" pain is actually "we have no internal boundaries" pain, and the cheaper fix is a modular monolith. You can get most of the benefits — clear ownership per module, enforced boundaries, independent reasoning — by organising the single deployable into modules with explicit interfaces and using architecture tests to forbid cross-module access to internals. This gives you clean seams without the network. Then, if and when a specific module demonstrably needs independent deployment, scaling, or fault isolation, you extract exactly that module along the seam you already created, and the extraction is cheap because the boundary already exists. So my answer to "would you split 300,000 lines?" is: not because of the number; I would first establish the boundaries internally, measure change coupling and ownership, and extract only the specific capabilities that have a proven independent need.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India one large core-banking service of three hundred thousand lines handles account management, transfers, loan origination, and regulatory reporting.

Problem 1 — the team feels the service is too big and wants to split it into four microservices immediately. But analysis of the commit history shows account management and transfers almost always change together, while regulatory reporting changes on a completely different cadence and is owned by a separate compliance team. This is exactly why we evaluate change coupling and ownership before splitting — reporting is a clean split candidate, but account and transfers are not.

Problem 2 — regulatory reporting runs heavy batch jobs that occasionally exhaust memory and slow down live transfers. This is exactly the blast-radius evidence that justifies isolating reporting into its own process.

Problem 3 — before any split, the team enforces internal module boundaries so that modules talk only through explicit interfaces, proving most of the "too big" pain was actually "no boundaries" pain. This is exactly the modular-monolith step that de-risks the eventual extraction.

The demo models the monolith as modules behind interfaces, computes a simple change-coupling and ownership score per module to recommend what to split, and shows reporting being isolated while account and transfers stay together.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is evidence for four modules of the three-hundred-thousand-line monolith: their change coupling with the core, whether ownership is clear, whether they can starve other capabilities, and whether they need independent scaling.

Step 1: The transfers module has a change coupling of 0.82 with the core, well above the 0.6 threshold, meaning it almost always changes together with core code. The advisor recommends keeping it in the monolith, because splitting it would spread a single logical change across two services.

Step 2: The accounts module similarly co-changes at 0.80, so it is also kept in the monolith. Transfers and accounts belong together.

Step 3: The reporting module has a low coupling of 0.15, a clear compliance owner, and it can starve other capabilities through heavy batch jobs plus it needs independent scaling. It satisfies the independent-change, clear-ownership, and fault-or-scale conditions, so the advisor recommends extracting it to its own service — this is the one true split candidate.

Step 4: The loan-origination module changes independently at 0.25 but has no clear owner. The advisor refuses to split it yet, recommending the team fix ownership first, because an extracted service with no owner becomes an orphan dependency.

Step 5: The conclusion is to extract only reporting and to strengthen internal boundaries for the rest, rather than performing a blind four-way split. The number three hundred thousand never entered the decision — the evidence did.

```
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO] === Split decision for 300K-line core-banking monolith ===
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO] KEEP transfers (co-changes with core 0.82)
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO]   → transfers: KEEP_IN_MONOLITH
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO] KEEP accounts (co-changes with core 0.8)
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO]   → accounts: KEEP_IN_MONOLITH
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO] SPLIT reporting (independent + fault/scale need)
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO]   → reporting: EXTRACT_TO_SERVICE
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [WARNING] KEEP loan-origination (no clear owner — would become an orphan)
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO]   → loan-origination: KEEP_FIX_OWNERSHIP_FIRST
2026-10-24 18:35:07 [INFO] Conclusion: extract 'reporting' only; modularize the rest internally
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
My first response to "the service is three hundred thousand lines, should we split it into microservices?" is that line count is not a reason to split. Size tells you the service is big; it does not tell you where the boundaries are or whether a network boundary would help. The decision has to follow evidence about coupling, ownership, blast radius, and scaling needs, because splitting is not free — it converts in-process method calls into network calls and imports a permanent tax that every future change and every incident will pay.

So before deciding I evaluate four things. First, change coupling: which modules change together in the same commits. If transfers and accounts almost always change together, splitting them spreads one logical change across two deployables and two pipelines, which makes every change slower and riskier, so those stay together. The good split candidates are modules that change independently of the rest, because only those actually gain independent deployment. Second, ownership: a split pays off when it aligns a service with a single team that can own and operate it, and if no team would clearly own the extracted service, the split just creates an orphan that everyone depends on and nobody maintains. Third, blast radius: does a failure or resource spike in one capability take down unrelated capabilities today — because that is real fault coupling a split could fix. Fourth, independent scaling: does one capability need to scale very differently from the rest.

Against all of that I weigh the microservices tax explicitly. Method calls become network calls that can be slow, fail, or time out, so I need retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers where there used to be a simple invocation. I need service discovery, distributed tracing to follow a request across processes, and I lose the single database transaction — a change that was atomic across two modules now spans two services and needs sagas, an outbox, and eventual consistency. That is not a one-time migration cost, it is an ongoing tax.

The insight I always offer is that most "we need microservices" pain is actually "we have no internal boundaries" pain, and the cheaper fix is a modular monolith. I organise the single deployable into modules with explicit interfaces and use architecture tests to forbid reaching into another module's internals, which gives me clear ownership, enforced boundaries, and independent reasoning without the network. Then, if a specific module demonstrably needs independent deployment, scaling, or fault isolation, I extract exactly that module along the seam I already built, and the extraction is cheap because the boundary already exists.

In the banking case I described, the evidence pointed to extracting only the regulatory reporting module — it changed on a separate cadence, had a clear compliance owner, ran heavy batch jobs that could starve live transfers, and needed its own scaling. Accounts and transfers co-changed constantly, so they stayed together, and loan-origination had no clear owner, so I would fix ownership before even considering it. So my answer is not "yes, split the three hundred thousand lines" and not "no, never" — it is "establish the boundaries internally, measure coupling and ownership, isolate the one capability that has a proven independent need, and leave the rest as a well-structured modular monolith."
